P, or polynomial time complexity class. The set of decision problems solvable by a deterministic algorithm in polynomial time. That is, in a number of steps bounded by a polynomial function of the input size. It represents the realm of computationally feasible or tractable problems and is one of the two central classes in the P versus NP problem, the most important open question in computer science. Understanding P is essential to grasping computational feasibility and the limits of known algorithms. P stands for polynomial time, and formally it is the set of decision problems, or languages, decidable by a deterministic Turing machine in O of n to the k time for some fixed constant k independent of the input n. A problem is in P if there exists an algorithm that, for any input of size n, returns a yes or no answer in at most c times n to the k steps for constants c and k. Deterministic means the Turing machine follows a unique computational path, unlike nondeterministic machines which explore multiple paths in parallel. The output is yes or no in a decision problem; optimization variants, where you find the best solution, are outside P by definition, though related. Let me give you some examples of P problems. Sorting: given an array, sort it in O of n log n time, as in merge sort or quicksort. Searching: given a sorted array and a target, find it via binary search in O of log n. Graph reachability: is there a path from vertex u to vertex v? Solvable in O of n plus m time via breadth-first search or depth-first search. Primality testing: is n prime? Solvable in polynomial time via the AKS primality test, though not the simplest method in practice. Integer multiplication: multiply two n-bit integers in O of n squared time, or faster via Karatsuba or Strassen algorithms. Greatest common divisor: the Euclidean algorithm computes it in O of log of the minimum of a and b time. Several important relationships hold between P and other complexity classes. P is a subset of NP: this is proven. Every problem solvable in polynomial time is also verifiable in polynomial time. If you can solve it, you can verify it. P is a subset of EXPTIME: polynomial-time problems are solved faster than exponential-time problems. NP is a subset of PSPACE: nondeterministic polynomial-time problems fit in polynomial space, often with exponential time. Whether P equals NP is open. It is unknown whether P equals NP. If true, then every verifiable problem is solvable, a revolutionary result that would break modern cryptography. The Millennium Prize Problem: the Clay Mathematics Institute offers a one million dollar reward for proving or disproving P equals NP. The cryptographic implications are profound. If P equals NP, then integer factorization, which underlies RSA encryption, would be solvable in polynomial time, destroying modern encryption. Conversely, if P does not equal NP, then one-way functions exist, justifying cryptography. Optimization implications: thousands of optimization problems, such as the knapsack problem, the traveling salesman problem, and graph coloring, are NP-complete. If P equals NP, all would be efficiently solvable. The practical assumption throughout cryptography, computational complexity theory, and algorithm research is that P does not equal NP, though this remains unproven. P is the foundation of computational feasibility. In the absence of the ability to run exponential-time algorithms, which blow up for n greater than twenty or thirty, polynomial time is the practical boundary of what is considered solvable in computer science. The class P emerged formally in the nineteen seventies, through the work of Cook and Karp, and immediately became central to understanding algorithm design and computational limits. The P versus NP problem captures the essential mystery: can verification, a seemingly easier task, be as hard as solving from scratch? If not, an enormous class of practical problems in optimization, constraint satisfaction, and combinatorial search would unlock. If yes, then cryptography and many heuristic algorithms are justified.
